sourceTitle: Watching the Sky, Interpreting the Odds
scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Advanced original Astronomy Reading test, expert content approval pending.

questions.q: Why is an asteroid's near-Earth label insufficient to establish danger?
choices: It is determined only by the rock's chemical composition.
It proves the object is closer than any communication satellite.
It describes orbital geometry rather than a predicted impact.
It refers exclusively to asteroids that have recently changed direction.
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph separates a geometrical classification from a judgement of danger.

questions.q: Where does the uncertainty about a distant asteroid primarily arise?
choices: From limitations in our observations of its present trajectory.
From the asteroid moving randomly between different orbits.
From the impossibility of using physics in space.
From the inability of telescopes to detect objects close to Earth.
questions.explanation: The writer says uncertainty is chiefly in what researchers know about the motion.

questions.q: How do infrared instruments improve the investigation of space objects?
choices: They reveal the precise composition of every asteroid.
They remove all uncertainty immediately after discovery.
They make optical observations unnecessary.
They can detect thermal emissions from objects difficult to see in reflected light.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph describes infrared and optical observations as complementary.

questions.q: Why might an estimated impact probability rise temporarily as data improve?
choices: Because the asteroid's orbit necessarily becomes more dangerous.
Because revised measurements can narrow the set of plausible future trajectories.
Because every additional measurement increases the object's speed.
Because scientists stop using their original calculations.
questions.explanation: The writer explains that updated observations change how likely trajectories fit the data.

questions.q: What is the strongest conclusion supported by the DART experiment?
choices: Every possible asteroid impact can now be prevented.
Asteroid composition never changes the outcome of a collision.
Momentum transfer can change an orbit under observed conditions.
The spacecraft achieved a complete mapping of Dimorphos.
questions.explanation: Paragraph three distinguishes an experimental result from a universal guarantee.

questions.q: Why can a modest change years in advance be preferable to a dramatic late action?
choices: Small early changes may accumulate into a safer future position.
Last-minute interventions require no knowledge of the target.
A spacecraft becomes more powerful the longer it waits.
The asteroid's material properties stop affecting its motion.
questions.explanation: The engineering discussion emphasises early detection and sufficient warning time.

questions.q: What made the physical effect of DART larger than its momentum alone suggested?
choices: Infrared measurements changed the meaning of the impact.
Dimorphos was already slowing down before the mission.
Didymos pulled the smaller asteroid much closer to Earth.
Ejected debris produced an additional push on Dimorphos.
questions.explanation: The debris plume contributed extra momentum beyond the collision itself.

questions.q: Why is the follow-up Hera mission relevant to the earlier experiment?
choices: It will turn the target into a stable planet.
It can examine the system's material properties and help explain the deflection.
It will replace the need for observations from Earth.
It is designed to repeat the same impact without new measurements.
questions.explanation: Paragraph four connects uncertainty about rubble-pile structure with Hera's investigation.

questions.q: Which pair of communication mistakes does the author identify?
choices: Reporting risk with numbers and reporting it with words.
Using optical and infrared observations together.
Treating every close approach as a crisis and ignoring rare risks.
Revising estimates and explaining why they changed.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph warns against both exaggerated alarm and dismissive complacency.

questions.q: What does the author imply about openness when a prediction changes?
choices: Public trust can grow when revisions and evidence are explained transparently.
Changes should be hidden until all debate has ended.
An updated estimate proves that the original researchers lacked competence.
The public should receive only the most reassuring figure.
questions.explanation: The conclusion links credible planetary defence to transparent, proportionate communication.
